1.open: When you have had a rough day, who is the first person you want to talk to, and what makes them easy to talk to?
questions: Paul calls God "the Father of compassion and the God of all comfort" (v. 3). When you think of comfort, what comes to mind first, and how does that compare with how you picture God?

Paul says God comforts us "so that we can comfort those in any trouble" (v. 4). Think of someone who helped you because they had been through something similar. What did they do or say that made a difference?
Paul tells them, "We were under a burden far beyond our ability to endure, so that we despaired even of life" (v. 8). What do you make of an apostle being this open about hitting bottom?

Paul says the point was "that we would not trust in ourselves, but in God, who raises the dead" (v. 9). When have you reached the end of your own strength? If trusting God feels hard or distant right now, what makes it so?
Paul says God will deliver "as you help us by your prayers" (v. 11). He asks for prayer and expects it to matter. Who prays for you, and who could you pray for?
In verses 15 to 17 some in Corinth accused Paul of being careless and unreliable because he changed his plans. How do you feel when people misjudge your motives, and how might Paul's response help?
Verse 22 says God "put His Spirit in our hearts as a pledge of what is to come." A pledge is like a down payment. What does it mean to you that God has started something he promises to finish?
1.life: Think of one person going through something you have been through. This week, send them a short message or offer to sit with them. You do not need to fix anything. Just let them know you understand.
1.prayer: Thank God that he is "the God of all comfort" (v. 3). Ask for the honesty to receive comfort when you need it and the willingness to pass it on to someone else.
1.tip: Verses 4 to 7 can be misused to tell hurting people that their pain is for someone else's benefit. Keep the focus on God comforting us in trouble, let people share at their own pace, and resist the urge to fix or explain anyone's suffering.

2.open: Have you ever had to wait anxiously for news from someone, and what did the waiting feel like?
questions: Paul says he wrote "through many tears" out of "great distress and anguish of heart" (v. 4). Why do you think he wanted them to know it was written in tears? Can love and hard words go together?

Paul says he wrote "not to grieve you but to let you know how much I love you" (v. 4). Think of a time someone told you something hard because they cared. How did you receive it then, and how do you see it now?

The church had disciplined a man who caused grief, and Paul says "The punishment imposed on him by the majority is sufficient for him" (v. 6). What do you think it means for a punishment to be enough? Who decides?
Paul urges them to "forgive and comfort him, so that he will not be overwhelmed by excessive sorrow" (v. 7). What might it look like for a church or a family to welcome someone back after real harm?
Verse 11 speaks of not letting Satan "outwit us." How could holding on to a grudge, or being harsh with someone who has failed, give something destructive room to grow?
Paul admits he "had no peace in my spirit" in Troas even though "a door stood open" (vv. 12, 13). Why might a good opportunity still leave someone restless? When has that been true for you?

Paul says we are "the sweet aroma of Christ" to some and "an odor that brings death" to others, then asks, "who is qualified for such a task?" (vv. 15, 16). How would you honestly answer that question today, including if you feel unqualified or unsure?
Paul says he does not "peddle the word of God for profit" but speaks "with sincerity" (v. 17). What does speaking about faith sincerely look like in everyday life, as opposed to selling it?
2.life: Think of one person you have been holding at arm's length because of an old hurt. This week, take one small step toward them that fits the situation, such as a message, a prayer for them by name, or a decision to stop rehearsing the offense. If the harm was serious or is ongoing, ask a trusted friend or pastor what a safe step looks like.
2.prayer: Thank God for forgiving us when we did not deserve it. Ask for wisdom and a soft heart toward anyone we find hard to forgive, and for honesty to speak about Christ with sincerity.
2.tip: Verses 5 to 8 can sting if someone in the group has been badly hurt or has been the one disciplined. Be clear that Paul is not telling anyone to ignore harm or return to an unsafe situation. He is asking a church to restore a person who has been held to account. Also note that Christians disagree about who the offender was and which letter Paul means, and leave it there, since the main point of the passage does not depend on settling it.

3.open: Who is someone whose life made you think, 'I want what they have'? What did you notice about them?
questions: Paul says the believers in Corinth are "our letter, inscribed on our hearts, known and read by everyone" (v. 2). If people read your life like a letter, what do you think it says?

Verse 3 says this letter is written "not with ink but with the Spirit of the living God, not on tablets of stone but on tablets of human hearts." Why would Paul's first readers, who knew the Ten Commandments on stone, find that picture striking?
Paul says, "our competence comes from God" (v. 5). Where do you feel not up to the task, at home, at work or in your faith? What changes if the ability comes from God and not from you?

Verse 6 says "the letter kills, but the Spirit gives life." Many readers take this to mean rules alone show our failure but cannot change us. Where have you seen the difference between living by rules and living by God's Spirit?
Paul argues that if the old way came with glory, the new is "even more glorious" (v. 8). Why might it matter to him to say that the old way was truly glorious and not simply bad?
Verse 17 says, "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is freedom." What does freedom look like in a Christian's life? What does it not look like?
Verse 18 says we "are being transformed into His image with intensifying glory." Where, if anywhere, have you seen slow change in yourself? If you haven't, what do you make of the word "being" here?
Verses 14 and 15 talk about a veil over hearts. Is there anything about God or the Bible that still feels covered or unclear to you right now? You can say so honestly.
3.life: This week, pick one person in your life and quietly pay attention to how God might be changing them or you. Thank God for one sign of change, however small, and tell the person if it fits.
3.prayer: Thank God that he writes on hearts and not only on stone. Ask the Spirit to give freedom and slow, real change to each person in the group.
3.tip: Verses 6 and 14 to 15 can be heard as putting down the Old Testament or Jewish people. Remind the group that Paul was a Jewish man speaking about his own people and that he calls the old way glorious. Say plainly that Christians differ on how the law relates to the new covenant, and keep the focus on the Spirit's work.

4.open: What is the most worn out, beat up thing you own that you still refuse to throw away?
questions: Paul says, "since God in His mercy has given us this ministry, we do not lose heart" (v. 1). What do you think keeps a person going when the work is hard and thankless?

Paul says he has renounced "secret and shameful ways" and speaks by "open proclamation of the truth" (v. 2). Why might honesty and openness matter so much when you are sharing something you care about?

Verse 4 says the minds of unbelievers have been blinded so they "cannot see the light of the gospel." Most readers take the "god of this age" to be Satan. How does this help or trouble you when you think about friends or family who do not believe?

Paul says, "we do not proclaim ourselves, but Jesus Christ as Lord" (v. 5). Where do you see people, in churches or anywhere else, drawing attention to themselves instead? How do we guard against that in our own lives?
Verse 7 says, "we have this treasure in jars of clay." What cracks or weaknesses in your life are hardest to accept, and how might God's power show up through them?

Paul lists being "hard pressed" but "not crushed" and "struck down, but not destroyed" (vv. 8-9). Which of these pairs sounds most like your life right now? If none do, which would you want to be true of you in a hard season?

Verse 16 says, "our outer self is wasting away, yet our inner self is being renewed day by day." What does being renewed on the inside look like in ordinary life? If you honestly don't feel it, what is that like?
In verse 18 Paul says, "we fix our eyes not on what is seen, but on what is unseen." What takes most of your attention each day, and what would it look like to give some of it to what lasts?
4.life: This week, pick one small thing that is wearing you down, and name it honestly to God each morning. Then ask one other person how they are really doing and listen without trying to fix it.
4.prayer: Thank God for making his light shine in our hearts. Ask him to be strong in the weak places of your lives, and to give each person in the group fresh hope for the week ahead.
4.tip: Verses 3 and 4 can sound harsh about people who do not believe, and the idea of Satan blinding minds may lead to heated or fearful talk. Keep the group on Paul's main point, that it is God who gives light, and remind everyone that Christians also disagree on whether this chapter's "we" describes Paul's own sufferings or a pattern for every believer. Name that in one line and move on.

5.open: What is something you have held onto for a long time, even though it was clearly wearing out?
questions: Paul calls our body an "earthly tent" that can be "dismantled" (v. 1). What does that picture say about how he sees this life, and how does it sit with you?
In verse 4 Paul says "we groan under our burdens." What is weighing on you or someone you love right now? You can answer as honestly as you like, including if hope feels hard.
Verse 5 says God "has given us the Spirit as a pledge of what is to come." What do you think it means to have a down payment on something not yet here?
Verse 7 says, "we walk by faith, not by sight." Where is it hardest for you to trust what you cannot see? What helps, even a little?
Verse 10 says we "must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ." How does that land with you, and how might it sit alongside Paul's words about reconciliation later in the chapter?
In verse 14 Paul says "Christ's love compels us." What tends to drive you most day to day, and how is that different from being compelled by love?

Verse 17 says, "if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation." What would it look like for something old in you to pass away and something new to begin? What would it look like to see another person that way?

Verse 21 describes God making Christ "to be sin on our behalf." Christians understand how this works in different ways. What does it mean to you that Christ took on our brokenness so we could be made right with God?
5.life: Paul says he no longer sizes people up by appearances. This week, pick one person you tend to judge by how they look, act or seem from the outside. Pray for them by name each day and ask God to show you how he sees them.
5.prayer: Thank God that he is "reconciling the world to Himself in Christ" and does not hold our wrongs against us. Ask him for comfort in the groaning and burdens of this life, and for hearts willing to pass that welcome on to others.
5.tip: Verse 10 can make some people anxious, while others hear it as a threat for someone else. Remind the group that Paul writes about judgment and about God not counting our trespasses in the same chapter. Let people name their honest fears about it without rushing to fix them. Also, Christians differ on how verse 21 works, so do not try to settle it tonight. Keep the focus on what the whole passage says: God has made the first move toward us.

6.open: Think of a time you were part of a team, a family or a group where you really felt you belonged. What made it feel that way?
questions: Paul urges the Corinthians "not to receive God's grace in vain" (v. 1). What do you think it looks like when someone receives grace but it makes no real difference in daily life?
Paul says, "now is the time of favor; now is the day of salvation!" (v. 2). What do you hear in that line, an invitation, a warning, or something else?

Instead of offering letters of recommendation, Paul points to "great endurance" in "troubles, hardships, and calamities" (v. 4). When has the way someone handled hard times made you trust them more, or less, than anything they said about themselves?
Paul describes himself as "sorrowful, yet always rejoicing" (v. 10). How can sorrow and joy sit side by side in a person? Have you known that in your own life?
Paul says, "Our hearts are open wide," and asks the Corinthians to "open wide your hearts also" (vv. 11, 13). Where is it hard for you to open up to other believers, and what makes it hard?

Verse 14 says, "Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers." Christians read this differently: some think of marriage, some of close partnerships, some of pagan worship. What do you think Paul is protecting, and what might it mean for how we treat neighbors and coworkers who don't share our faith?
Paul says, "we are the temple of the living God" (v. 16). What changes if God lives among his people and not only in a building?

God promises, "I will be a Father to you, and you will be My sons and daughters" (v. 18). If you are unsure about God or find that promise hard to believe, what makes it hard to take in? There is no wrong answer here.
6.life: Pick one person in your church or group you have kept at a distance, and take one small step to open your heart to them this week: a message, a coffee, or an honest question. Then notice how you spend your time and ask whether any close commitment is pulling you away from God.
6.prayer: Thank God that now is "the day of salvation" and that his grace is not wasted on you. Ask for open hearts toward one another and for wisdom about the people and things you let shape you.
6.tip: Verses 14 to 18 can easily turn into a debate about who we are allowed to be friends with or marry. Say plainly that Christians read the passage differently, then steer back to Paul's main point: God's people belong to God and are loved by him. Remind the group that Paul himself spent his life reaching people outside the faith.

7.open: Can you remember a time you got an apology or a hard word from someone and were glad about it later?
questions: Paul begins with "these promises" and then calls them to "cleanse ourselves from everything that defiles body and spirit" (v. 1). Why do you think he puts God's promises first and the call to change second?
Paul admits that in Macedonia there were "conflicts on the outside, fears within" (v. 5). What does it tell you that an apostle was this worn down and afraid?
Verse 6 says "God, who comforts the downcast, comforted us by the arrival of Titus." Where has God's comfort come to you through another person?
Paul says he "did regret" sending his hard letter, and yet now he does not (v. 8). What makes it so hard to say a painful thing to someone we care about?
Verse 10 says "Godly sorrow brings repentance that leads to salvation without regret, but worldly sorrow brings death." In your own words, what is the difference between the two?
Paul lists what their sorrow produced, including "what earnestness" and "what longing" (v. 11). What does real change look like when it is more than just feeling bad?
When you think about your own failures, do you find it easier to feel crushed, to shrug them off, or to turn toward God? Be as honest as you can, including if you are not sure what to do with guilt.
Paul found great joy in restored friendship (vv. 13 to 16). Is there a relationship in your life that needs a hard conversation or a fresh start, and what might the first small step be?
7.life: This week, pick one thing you feel bad about, whether toward God or toward a person. Ask yourself if the sorrow is leading you toward change or only leaving you stuck. Then take one small, concrete step, such as an honest prayer or an apology.
7.prayer: Thank God that he comforts the downcast. Ask him to give us sorrow that leads toward him and not toward shame, and to help us make things right where we can.
7.tip: Verse 10 can be heard as pressure to feel bad enough. Keep it gentle: godly sorrow is not measured by how upset we get, but by whether it turns us toward God and toward change. Also, be ready for someone who carries heavy guilt, and remind the group that the chapter is full of comfort.

8.open: Think of a time someone helped you when you really needed it. What did they do, and how did it make you feel?
questions: Paul says the Macedonian churches had a "terrible ordeal" and "deep poverty," yet their "abundant joy" overflowed "into rich generosity" (v. 2). What surprises you about that combination?
The Macedonians "earnestly pleaded with us for the privilege of sharing" (v. 4). When have you seen giving treated as a privilege rather than a burden, and what made the difference?
Paul writes, "I am not giving a command, but I am testing the sincerity of your love" (v. 8). Why do you think he chooses to invite rather than order?
Verse 9 says Jesus "though He was rich, yet for your sake He became poor." How does this change the way you think about giving?

Verse 12 says the gift is acceptable "according to what one has, not according to what he does not have." How does this land if money is tight for you right now? Be as honest as you like, including if it feels hard to hear.

Paul wants "equality," where "your surplus will meet their need" and later theirs may meet yours (vv. 13, 14). Christians differ on whether this is a lasting principle or mainly about one particular crisis. What do you make of it, and what would sharing look like for a group like ours?

Paul sends trusted people with the money so there is no "criticism of the way we administer this generous gift" (v. 20). Why does he care how things look to people as well as to God? How does that apply to churches and charities today?
Corinth had started well but had not finished (vv. 10, 11). What is something good you began, in your faith or your life, that you would like to follow through on?
8.life: Pick one practical way to share what you have this week. It might be money, a meal, time or a skill, given to someone in need. Keep it within your means, as verse 12 says, and do it quietly and gladly.
8.prayer: Thank God for the grace of Jesus, who became poor so that we could share in his riches. Ask for open hands, an honest look at your own needs, and the eagerness to finish what you have started.
8.tip: Talk of giving can make people feel guilty or embarrassed, especially anyone short on money. Point the group to verses 8 and 12: Paul is not commanding or shaming anyone, and a gift counts by what a person has. Keep the focus on Jesus in verse 9, and avoid asking anyone to share what they personally give.

9.open: Think of a gift you gave or received that you still remember. What made it stick with you?
questions: Paul tells the Corinthians he has been boasting about their eagerness, and that their "zeal has stirred most of them to do likewise" (v. 2). Who has stirred you to be more generous, and how did they do it?
Paul sends the brothers ahead so the gift will be ready "generously and not begrudgingly" (v. 5). Why might it matter to him how the gift is given and not only how much?

Paul says, "Whoever sows sparingly will also reap sparingly, and whoever sows generously will also reap generously" (v. 6). What do you think he means by the harvest here? Christians read this differently, some seeing material reward and others seeing growth in goodness and the ability to keep giving.
Verse 7 says to give what you have decided in your heart, "not out of regret or compulsion." Where have you felt pressure around giving, and what did that do to you?

Paul writes that "God is able to make all grace abound to you, so that in all things, at all times, having all that you need, you will abound in every good work" (v. 8). If you are honest, how easy is it for you to believe you have enough to share? You can say it is hard.

Verse 12 says the gift is "not only supplying the needs of the saints" but also leads to thanksgiving to God. Can you think of a time when help you gave or received led to gratitude beyond the money or the meal?
Paul ends with "Thanks be to God for His indescribable gift!" (v. 15). Most Christians read this as Jesus. How might remembering what God has already given change the way we think about giving?
9.life: Decide ahead of time on one gift this week, of money, time or practical help, and give it without needing anyone to notice. If giving feels hard right now, spend a few minutes telling God honestly where you feel tight or afraid.
9.prayer: Thank God for his indescribable gift. Ask him to loosen fear and pressure around giving, and to help each person in the group give freely and gladly in the ways that fit their season of life.
9.tip: Giving can bring up shame or money stress, and some may have been pressured by churches in the past. Say up front that this study is not a call to give more or to compare. Keep the focus on verse 7, that giving is a free decision of the heart, and let people pass on questions that feel too personal.

10.open: Who is someone you first judged by how they looked or sounded, and then you found out you were wrong about them?
questions: Paul begins by appealing "by the mildness and gentleness of Christ" (v. 1). Why might he start there when he is being criticized? What does it tell you about how he wants to handle the conflict?
His critics said he was "humble when face to face" but "bold when away" (v. 1). Have you ever been misjudged because of your personality or style? How did it feel?

Paul says, "we do not wage war according to the flesh" and that his weapons "have divine power to demolish strongholds" (vv. 3, 4). What do you think it looks like to push back on a bad idea without using pressure, spin or force?
Verse 5 speaks of taking "captive every thought to make it obedient to Christ." What kinds of thoughts tend to run unchecked in your head? What helps you slow them down?

Christians read the "strongholds" of verses 4 and 5 differently. Some see mainly proud human arguments, others see unseen evil powers. However you read it, what do you think Paul wants the Corinthians to do?
Paul says his critics were "looking at outward appearances" (v. 7). Where do you see people today trusting the polished and impressive over the plain and faithful? When have you done it yourself?

Paul will only boast "within the field of influence that God has assigned to us" (v. 13). What has God put in front of you, such as your family, work, church or neighborhood? How do you tell the difference between faithful work there and chasing credit?

Verse 18 says, "it is not the one who commends himself who is approved, but the one whom the Lord commends." If you honestly doubt that God approves of you, or aren't sure what that would even mean, what comes up when you read this?
10.life: This week, notice once when you are tempted to judge someone by how they look or sound, or to pump up your own image. Pause, and ask God to help you see that person, or yourself, the way he does.
10.prayer: Ask God to free you from needing everyone's approval. Pray for the humility to "boast in the Lord" (v. 17) and for the patience to treat quiet, faithful people with respect.
10.tip: Verses 3 to 6 use war language, and some people may take it as permission to be harsh with others, or may bring up spiritual warfare teachings. Acknowledge that Christians read the "strongholds" differently, then steer back to what the text clearly says: Paul's weapons are truth and gentleness, not force.

11.open: What is the most embarrassing way you ever got out of a tight spot?
questions: Paul says he is jealous for the Corinthians "with a godly jealousy" (v. 2). What does it look like when someone cares about you that much, and when does that kind of care feel like too much?
He fears their minds "may be led astray from your simple and pure devotion to Christ" (v. 3). What does simple devotion to Christ look like in everyday life, and what tends to complicate it?

In verse 4 Paul says the Corinthians "put up with it very easily" when someone preaches a different Jesus. Where do you see teaching today that sounds close to the real thing but is not quite? How could we tell the difference?

Paul preached to them "free of charge" and says it was out of love (vv. 7, 11). Some in Corinth seem to have taken it badly. Why might a gift or a sacrifice be misunderstood, and have you ever been on either side of that?
Verse 14 says "Satan himself masquerades as an angel of light." Why can harmful influence look attractive or even religious? What helps us stay alert without becoming suspicious of everyone?
Paul lists beatings, shipwrecks, hunger and danger instead of achievements (vv. 23-27). Why might he choose those as his proof, and how does that compare to what we usually put on a résumé?
Beyond all that, he carries "the pressure of my concern for all the churches" (v. 28). Who or what do you carry worry for, and where do you take it?

Paul ends with the story of being lowered in a basket to escape (vv. 32, 33), and says he will boast "of the things that show my weakness" (v. 30). What is something weak or unimpressive in your life that you find hard to talk about? What would it take to say it out loud, even to God?
11.life: This week, share one honest struggle or failure with a trusted friend instead of only the good news. Notice how it feels, and how they respond.
11.prayer: Ask God to keep your devotion to Christ simple and true. Ask for the humility to be honest about your weaknesses and for wisdom to tell what is genuine from what only looks impressive.
11.tip: Verses 13 to 15 can turn into a hunt for who the false teachers are today. Keep the group on the passage: Paul's concern is for the Corinthians' devotion to Jesus. Note that Christians differ on exactly who his rivals were, then steer toward the question of how each of us tests what we hear, starting with ourselves.

12.open: What is something you tried for a long time to fix or change about yourself, and what happened?
questions: Paul describes being "caught up to Paradise" and hearing things "that man is not permitted to tell" (v. 4). Why do you think he shares this so briefly and so reluctantly?

Paul says he was given "a thorn in my flesh" "to keep me from becoming conceited" (v. 7). What do you think it feels like to carry something painful that never goes away? What might it do to a person?

Paul writes, "Three times I pleaded with the Lord to take it away from me" (v. 8). Have you ever prayed hard for something and gotten a different answer than you hoped for? Tell us as much or as little as you like.
The Lord answers, "My grace is sufficient for you, for My power is perfected in weakness" (v. 9). What does this mean to you, and is there any part of it you find hard to accept?
Paul says, "For when I am weak, then I am strong" (v. 10). How is this different from simply putting up with hard things or pretending they are fine?

In verse 14 Paul says he is not seeking "your possessions, but you," and in verse 15 he will "most gladly spend my money and myself." What does this show about how he sees the Corinthians, and what does it look like to love people this way today?

Paul fears finding "quarreling, jealousy, rage, rivalry, slander, gossip" when he arrives (v. 20). Which of these do churches and small groups find easiest to slide into, and what helps guard against it?
If you are honest, where do you feel weak, limited or worn out right now? What would it look like to bring that to God without dressing it up?
12.life: Pick one weakness or limit you usually hide or fight against. This week, tell God about it plainly each day, and tell one trusted person too. Notice what changes, even if the weakness stays.
12.prayer: Thank God that his grace is enough and that his power meets us in weakness. Pray for anyone in the group who is carrying a long-term struggle, and ask for honesty and patience with each other.
12.tip: Be careful with verses 7 to 10. Christians differ on whether God sends suffering for our good or only allows it and works through it, and on whether we should expect to live with some afflictions rather than be healed. Someone in the room may be in real pain or praying for healing. Avoid tidy answers, say plainly that Paul's thorn is unexplained, and let people stay with the hard question.

13.open: When was the last time someone asked you to prove something, and how did it go?
questions: Paul says he is coming a third time and will "not spare anyone" (v. 2). Why do you think he warns them ahead of time instead of simply showing up?
Some in Corinth were demanding proof that Christ was speaking through Paul (v. 3). Why might they have doubted him, and what would it take for you to trust a leader?
Paul says Jesus "was indeed crucified in weakness, yet He lives by God's power" (v. 4). How does weakness fit with God's power in the story of Jesus?

Verse 5 says, "Examine yourselves to see whether you are in the faith." Christians read this either as a check on whether their own faith is real, or as Paul's reply that their faith proves his work was genuine. Which way do you lean, and why?
Paul wants them to do what is right "even if we appear to have failed" (v. 7). When have you cared more about doing right than about looking good?
Paul says his authority is for "building you up, not for tearing you down" (v. 10). How can you tell the difference between correction that builds up and correction that tears down?
In verse 11 Paul asks them to "encourage one another" and "live in peace." What is one thing that makes that hard in a group of people, and what helps?
Think about the closing blessing of "grace," "love" and "fellowship" (v. 14). Which of those three do you most need to hear tonight, even if you are not sure what you believe?
13.life: This week, take ten quiet minutes to ask yourself honestly where your faith stands, with no pressure to have it all sorted. Then tell God what you found, and send an encouraging message to one person in this group.
13.prayer: Ask God for honesty about where each person really is with him. Thank him for grace, love and fellowship, and pray for peace among the people in your group.
13.tip: Verse 5 can leave anxious people wondering if they have "failed the test." Say plainly that Christians read this verse differently, and remind the group that Paul writes it to people he calls family and closes with grace. Keep the tone gentle and give quiet members room to pass.
